# Microporous Water: Aqueous Fluids with High Gas Solubilities

Daniel P. Erdosy,1† Malia B. Wenny,1† Joy Cho,1† Christopher DelRe,1 Miranda V. Walter,1

Ricardo Sanchez,1 Yifeng Peng,2,3 Brian D. Polizzotti,2,3 Jarad A. Mason1*

1Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, United States. 2Division of Basic Cardiovascular Research, Department of Cardiology, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA 02115, United States. 3Department of Pediatrics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, United States. †These authors contributed equally to this work. *Corresponding author. Email: mason@chemistry.harvard.edu.

Liquids with permanent microporosity can absorb larger quantities of gas molecules than 1

conventional solvents1, providing new opportunities for liquid-phase gas storage, transport, 2

and reactivity. Current approaches to designing porous liquids rely on sterically bulky 3

solvent molecules or surface ligands and thus are not amenable to many important solvents, 4

including water2–4. Here, we report a generalizable thermodynamic strategy to create 5

permanent microporosity and high gas solubilities in liquid water. Specifically, we show how 6

the external and internal surface chemistry of microporous zeolite and metal–organic 7

framework nanocrystals can be tailored to promote the formation of stable dispersions in 8

water while maintaining dry networks of micropores that are accessible to gas molecules. As 9

a result of their permanent microporosity, these aqueous fluids can concentrate gases, 10

including oxygen (O2) and carbon dioxide (CO2), to much higher densities than are found in 11

typical aqueous environments. When these fluids are oxygenated, record-high capacities of 12

O2 can be delivered to hypoxic red blood cells, highlighting one potential application of this 13

new class of microporous liquids for physiological gas transport. 14

Water is the ubiquitous solvent for all biological processes and for many of the chemical 15

transformations critical to sustainable energy generation, storage, and utilization. Its polarity and 16

propensity for hydrogen bonding promote the solvation of polar substances but inhibit the 17

dissolution of nonpolar ones, including most gases5. The low solubility of gases in water—often 18

an order of magnitude less than in common organic solvents—imposes fundamental limitations on 19

many biomedical and energy-related technologies that require the transport of gas molecules 20

through aqueous fluids. For instance, low densities of dissolved O2 hinder tissue engineering and 21

cell culture in vitro and make it challenging to treat various types of life-threatening hypoxia in 22

vivo6. Aqueous-phase gas transport also limits the performance of fuel cells and the space-time 23

yield and efficiency of many important electrocatalytic reactions—including CO2 reduction, N2 24

reduction, and CH4 oxidation7. 25

Owing to their high internal surface areas and pore volumes, microporous solids can 26

concentrate gas molecules through adsorption to far higher densities than can be dissolved within 27

a typical liquid solvent—or than exist in a bulk gas phase—at a given temperature and pressure8. 28

Recently, it has been shown that permanent microporosity is not exclusively a feature of solid- 29

state materials and can be extended to the liquid phase in a nascent class of materials known as 30

porous liquids1. All porous liquids developed to date consist of microporous nanocrystals or 31

organic cage molecules dispersed in bulky organic solvents or ionic liquids that are too large to 32

diffuse through the pore entrances, leaving the micropores vacant and accessible to gas 33

molecules2-4. Because of their intrinsic microporosity, these liquids can store much higher 34

quantities of gas molecules than the corresponding nonporous liquid9. This sterics-based approach 35

to creating permanent microporosity within liquids is not, however, transferable to aqueous 36

systems because a micropore that is large enough to adsorb nearly any gas molecule will also be 37

large enough to accommodate H2O molecules. 38

Certain proteins and molecular cavitands contain pores that are accessible to H2O molecules 39

but remain dry in aqueous solution due to the presence of hydrophobic side chains or functional 40

groups that impart a thermodynamic penalty for H2O molecules residing within the pore instead 41

of within the bulk liquid10,11. Taking inspiration from these systems, we pursued a new strategy to 42

create liquids with permanent microporosity and high gas sorption capacities based on 43

thermodynamics rather than sterics. Specifically, we hypothesized that microporous nanocrystals 44

with hydrophobic internal surfaces and hydrophilic external surfaces could be designed to form 45

uniform, stable dispersions in water within which it is more thermodynamically favorable for water 46

to interact with other water molecules in the bulk liquid phase than to fill the microporous 47

networks—leaving them permanently dry and available to adsorb gas molecules (Fig. 1a). 48

Many zeolites and metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) can be synthesized with hydrophobic 49

pore surfaces and in nanocrystalline form12–14, making these materials an ideal—and highly 50

tunable—platform to target aqueous solutions with permanent microporosity. Moreover, solid 51

powders of several hydrophobic zeolites and MOFs have been shown to exclude liquid water from 52

their micropores at ambient pressure and temperature15. For instance, hydrostatic pressures in 53

excess of 900 bar must be applied to force water into the micropores of the pure-silica zeolite MFI 54

(silicalite-1) at 25 °C16. High pressures are required because water intrusion into silicalite-1 is 55

entropically disfavored since confined H2O molecules have less mobility than bulk H2O molecules 56

and endothermic since surface–H2O interactions are too weak to compensate for the hydrogen 57

bonding interactions between H2O molecules that are lost during intrusion17. Pressures of at least 58

200 bar are also required to force water into the micropores of other pure-silica zeolites and 59

hydrophobic zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs)15,18. The work that must be performed to 60

induce water intrusion into hydrophobic microporous solids has been leveraged for mechanical 61

energy storage and shock absorption16,19, but this phenomenon also offers an unexplored pathway 62

to create permanent and accessible microporosity in aqueous solutions—provided stable colloidal 63

solutions of such materials can be formed in a manner that does not alter the underlying 64

thermodynamic driving force for the constituent microporous networks to remain dry and adsorb 65

gas molecules. 66

Although hydrophobic materials are not generally dispersible in water, pure-silica zeolites 67

present a unique combination of hydrophobic internal pore surfaces templated by SiO4 tetrahedra, 68

which should prevent water intrusion, and hydrophilic external surfaces composed of terminal 69

silanols, which should promote water dispersibility for sufficiently small particles (Fig. 1c). With 70

an internal BET surface area of 457 m2/g (839 m2/mL) and established routes to produce uniform 71

nanocrystals of variable sizes (Extended Data Fig. 3, Supplementary Fig. 3)20,21, we therefore 72

anticipated that silicalite-1 would serve as a particularly promising candidate to generate aqueous 73

solutions with permanent microporosity and high gas capacities. Even though it does not contain 74

any inherently strong gas adsorption sites, silicalite-1 adsorbs over 230 times the amount of O2 75

and 90 times the amount of CO2 in the solid state as can be dissolved in water on a volumetric 76

basis at 1 bar and 25 °C (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Table 8). In addition, NMR experiments have 77

suggested that at least some fraction of silicalite-1 micropores are accessible to hyperpolarized Xe 78

in water22. 79

To create uniform, stable colloidal solutions of silicalite-1 in water and evaluate their 80

permanent microporosity, we first optimized synthesis, purification, and calcination conditions to 81

form nanocrystals of similar size (average diameter = 59 ± 8 nm or 90 ± 16 nm) and to remove 82

structure-directing tetrapropylammonium cations from the zeolite micropores without irreversibly 83

aggregating the particles in the solid state. The resulting silicalite-1 nanocrystals yielded 84

translucent aqueous colloidal solutions that were exceptionally stable, with no settling or 85

aggregation observed over the course of at least several weeks (Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 8). 86

Moreover, colloidal stability was not impacted by degassing the solutions under vacuum. If the 87

microporous networks of the silicalite-1 nanocrystals in these degassed solutions do not contain 88

water, the most concentrated colloidal solution (25 vol %, 38 wt %) would be 8.3% porous. 89

Since the volume occupied by a porous liquid with dry (air-filled) micropores will be larger 90

than the volume occupied by an equivalent nonporous liquid with wet (solvent-filled) micropores, 91

micropores in colloidal solutions. Excitingly, experimental densities at 15, 25, and 37 °C and 93

across a wide range of silicalite-1 concentrations are within 0.5% of the values predicted for dry 94

micropores using the crystallographic density and measured solid-state pore volume of silicalite-1 95

(Fig. 2a, Extended Data Fig. 1). This is in contrast to colloidal solutions of silicalite-1 in ethanol— 96

where intrusion of the less polar solvent molecules should be thermodynamically favored at 97

ambient pressure—and of the hydrophilic zeolite LTL in water—where water intrusion into the 98

more polar aluminosilicate pores should also be thermodynamically favored under ambient 99

conditions—which both have densities consistent with nonporous liquids containing solvent-filled 100

micropores (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1). Note that the density of solvent within a microporous 101

network is expected to be as much as 40% lower than the bulk liquid density due to confinement 102

effect23. 103

In order for a microporous liquid to be useful for gas storage, separation, and transport 104

applications, the pore networks need to be not only dry but also capable of reversibly adsorbing 105

and desorbing gas molecules. To directly probe the gas accessibility of micropores in water, we 106

measured the amount of O2 and CO2 absorbed in degassed solutions. At 25 °C, the gas absorption 107

capacity of a 12 vol % (20 wt %) colloidal solution of silicalite-1 nanocrystals was 26 mmol O2/L 108

at 0.84 bar and 284 mmol CO2/L at 0.67 bar, which is over an order of magnitude more than the 109

1.1 mmol/L of O2 and 23 mmol/L of CO2 absorbed in water under the same conditions (Fig. 3a, 110

b). Moreover, these gas capacities are 88% and 86%, respectively, of the O2 and CO2 capacities 111

predicted by assuming that solution absorption is equivalent to the sum of the pure-water gas 112

solubility and the adsorption capacity of silicalite-1 nanocrystals in the solid state (Fig. 3c). Since 113

the solid-state gas capacity measured for nanocrystalline powders will also include contributions 114

from gas adsorption at external surfaces and in interparticle voids that will not be present in 115

solution, these gas capacities are consistent with dry microporous networks in liquid water that are 116

fully accessible to gas molecules (Extended Data Fig. 5). In contrast to silicalite-1, the amount of 117

O2 and CO2 absorbed in a 5.1 vol % (9.5 wt%) aqueous solution of zeolite LTL nanocrystals is 118

nearly identical to pure water and corresponds to less than 2% of the zeolite capacity predicted for 119

dry micropores (Fig. 3). These results emphasize the importance of hydrophobic micropores and 120

permanent microporosity to achieving high gas capacities in water. 121

Cycling experiments confirm that gas absorption in silicalite-1 colloidal solutions is fully 122

reversible over at least 3 cycles of absorption followed by desorption under vacuum (Extended 123

Data Fig. 6). In addition, gas desorption was directly quantified by measuring the change in the 124

adsorbed O2 from the silicalite-1 nanocrystals into bulk water. This process continues until the 127

Consistent with the absorption experiments, oxygenated silicalite-1 solutions deliver up to 89% of 129

water (Fig. 4b). Moreover, the amount of dissolved O2 equilibrates within seconds after injection 131

of a silicalite-1 solution, which demonstrates the rapid gas desorption kinetics of these 132

microporous liquids (Fig. 4a). 133

The thermodynamic approach described here to designing microporous liquids is not specific 134

to silicalite-1 and is generalizable to a wide range of hydrophobic microporous materials. For 135

instance, there are currently over 50 known pure-silica zeolites and many other high-silica zeolites 136

that should be hydrophobic enough to exclude water in colloidal solutions24. Beyond zeolites, 137

metal–organic frameworks offer access to even higher internal surface areas and gas capacities, 138

along with substantially more structural and chemical diversity25. Most hydrophobic MOFs, 139

however, have relatively hydrophobic external surfaces and are not inherently dispersible in water. 140

Many hydrophobic MOFs are also prone to hydrolysis, particularly at low concentrations. This is 141

true for the isostructural hydrophobic frameworks Zn(mIm)2 (ZIF-8; mIm = 2-methylimidazolate) 142

and Co(mIm)2 (ZIF-67)26 (Fig. 1d)—nanocrystals of which rapidly aggregate in water and may 143

degrade if a large excess of water is present. Surface functionalization strategies can be applied to 144

disperse and stabilize hydrophobic MOFs in water27,28, providing a route to aqueous MOF 145

solutions with permanent microporosity as long as surface ligands can be selected that promote 146

dispersibility without infiltrating—or blocking access to—the framework micropores. 147

Noncovalent surface functionalization with macromolecules such as polyethylene glycol 148

(PEG) represents a simple approach for dispersing nanocrystals in solvents that would otherwise 149

induce aggregation and precipitation. Indeed, PEG (Mn = 35,000 g/mol) at 30 wt % in water can 150

disperse 20 wt % (21 vol %) of ZIF-8 nanocrystals (average size = 103 ± 10 nm) and 7.0 wt % (7.4 151

vol %) of ZIF-67 particles (average size = 780 ± 14 nm) without observable aggregation. 152

Furthermore, ZIF-8 remains crystalline when associated with PEG in water for at least 5 weeks, 153

and PEG increases the hydrolytic stability of ZIF-67, which otherwise rapidly degrades in water 154

(Extended Data Fig. 8). However, the measured O2 capacities of the PEG/ZIF-8 and PEG/ZIF-67 155

colloidal solutions are less than 15% of the expected capacities for ZIF particles with empty and 156

accessible microporous networks (Fig. 4b). Along with density measurements (Fig. 2b), these 157

limited O2 capacities suggest that the colloidal PEG/ZIF solutions are not porous because of 158

PEG—and perhaps H2O—intrusion into the ZIF micropores. Given that PEG is a compact, flexible 159

polymer and is amphiphilic, there does not appear to be a strong enough driving force to prevent 160

its intrusion by either sterics or thermodynamics—an effect that has been observed in the solid 161

state for PEG with other MOFs29. 162

As an alternative to synthetic polymers, we hypothesized that globular water-soluble proteins 163

could serve as promising macromolecules for non-covalent ZIF surface functionalization due to 164

their large size, conformational rigidity, and propensity to adsorb on hydrophobic surfaces30. We 165

identified bovine serum albumin (BSA) as an initial target for adsorbing onto ZIF-8 and ZIF-67 166

external surfaces because of its large diameter (~7 nm) and 17 permanent disulfide linkages that 167

minimize its conformational flexibility—the combination of which should sterically preclude 168

protein intrusion into the ZIF framework and preserve permanent microporosity (Fig. 1d). As 169

anticipated, mixing BSA (10 wt %) with ZIF-67 particles (3.3 wt %) enables complete dispersion 170

of ZIF-67 in water with no observable precipitation or degradation over a period of at least 8 days 171

(Fig. 1f, Extended Data Fig. 8), and density measurements are consistent with air-filled pores (Fig. 172

2a). Moreover, the measured O2 capacities of BSA/ZIF-67 colloidal solutions are 80% ± 9% of the 173

theoretical capacities obtained by assuming all ZIF-67 pores are empty and accessible to gas 174

molecules (Fig. 4a, b). Thus, non-covalent protein adsorption successfully extends the 175

microporous water concept to hydrophobic MOFs. 176

In addition to non-covalent approaches, covalent surface functionalization offers the potential 177

for strongly bound and precisely located surface ligands that promote water dispersibility at lower 178

loadings than more weakly associated surface ligands (Fig 1d)28,31. For covalent functionalization 179

to lead to a microporous liquid, the surface ligand must be hydrophilic enough—and present at a 180

high enough density—to promote water dispersibility, while short enough or bulky enough to 181

prevent pore infiltration. Moreover, functionalization must be confined to the external surface of 182

the nanocrystal and not inhibit gas accessibility to the internal pore surfaces. Though 183

functionalization with carbene surface ligands has been used to disperse ZIF nanocrystals in large 184

cyclic organic solvents to form organic microporous liquids32, the reactivity of carbenes makes 185

this synthetic strategy difficult to adapt to water. As an alternative approach, we anticipated that 186

mIm surface ligands would be nucleophilic enough to open epoxide rings and form a 187

β-hydroxyalkyl covalent linkage to the ZIF surface (Fig. 1d)33. Based on this reasoning, we reacted 188

ZIF-8 nanocrystals with methoxypolyethylene epoxide (mPEG; Mn = 750 g/mol for PEG). The 189

formation of the expected covalent linkage between the ring-opened epoxide and mIm was 190

indicating that approximately 10% of the mIm surface ligands are functionalized with mPEG 192

(Supplementary Fig. 21). Importantly, this grafting density (0.8 ligands per nm2) is sufficient to 193

stabilize colloidal solutions of ZIF-8 in water at up to 8.3 vol % (7.0 wt %), with minimal 194

precipitation or aggregation over the course of at least 5 days (Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 8B). In 195

contrast to ZIF-8 nanocrystals non-covalently functionalized with PEG, the solution density as a 196

function of concentration is consistent with that expected for a microporous liquid containing air- 197

filled pores (Fig. 2a), and the measured O2 capacity is 96% ± 7% of the theoretical amount (Fig. 198

4a, b). These results demonstrate that localization of short hydrophilic ligands on the surface of 199

hydrophobic MOF nanocrystals can impart dispersibility in water while maintaining permanent 200

The high gas capacities of the microporous liquids reported here present intriguing possibilities 202

for in vitro or in vivo O2 delivery, among others. Nature evolved intricate and tightly regulated 203

systems to transport O2 in water over hundreds of millions of years, and it is challenging to deliver 204

enough O2 to prevent hypoxia when these systems are absent or fail. A variety of natural and 205

synthetic gas carriers—including cell-free hemoglobin, heme mimics, perfluorocarbon emulsions, 206

and lipid- or polymer-coated microbubbles—have been explored to deliver O2 from aqueous 207

fluids, but overcoming issues that include limited gas-carrying capacity, poor control over release 208

kinetics, lack of reversibility, large particle sizes, dose-limiting toxicity, and long-term stability 209

remains an unsolved challenge6,34. As a result, there are currently no FDA-approved injectable 210

sources of O2 or artificial blood substitutes despite decades of research. 211

When oxygenated at 1 bar and 25 °C, blood has an O2 carrying capacity near 24 mL/dL 212

(assuming 15 g Hb/dL), which is an order of magnitude larger than the 2.9 mL/dL that can be 213

dissolved in pure H2O. Among non-covalent O2 carriers, lipid-coated microbubble dispersions 214

(90 vol %) have been demonstrated with irreversible O2 capacities that approach the gas-phase 215

density of O2 (91 mL/dL), while concentrated perfluorocarbon emulsions (60 vol %) have reached 216

reversible O2 capacities as high as 17 mL/dL (Fig. 4c)34,35. Microporous liquids offer a pathway to 217

reversible O2 capacities that far exceed these values, which would allow larger amounts of O2 to 218

be delivered from smaller volumes of an aqueous fluid. In particular, since silicalite-1 and ZIF-8 219

nanocrystals adsorb 731 mL/dL and 241 mL/dL of O2, respectively, in the solid state, low- 220

concentration aqueous solutions should be able to store and deliver exceptionally high densities of 221

O2. Indeed, a 6.6 vol % solution of (mPEG)ZIF-8 nanocrystals has a measured O2 carrying 222

capacity that is similar to many perfluorocarbon emulsions, which have concentrations of at least 223

20 vol % (Fig. 4c). Moreover, at a concentration of just 3.6 vol %, our aqueous solution of 90-nm 224

silicalite-1 nanocrystals has a measured reversible O2 capacity of 23 ± 2 mL/dL, matching that of 225

blood (Extended Data Table 1). At a concentration of 12.5 vol %, this O2 carrying capacity 226

increases to 89 ± 10 mL/dL, which is comparable to the density of bulk O2 gas (Fig. 4b). Though 227

higher concentration solutions of silicalite-1 nanocrystals tended to gel, we found that nanocrystals 228

of the zeolite ZSM-5—which is the isostructural aluminosilicate analogue of silicalite-1—have 229

more hydrophilic external surfaces than silicalite-1 nanocrystals (zeta potential of ZSM-5 and 230

silicalite-1 are –49.1 mV and –38.7, respectively). As a result, we were able to form a stable 231

colloidal solution of ZSM-5 nanocrystals (average diameter = 238 ± 23 nm; Si/Al = 64) in water 232

at a concentration of 37 vol % that had a viscosity of only 57 cP at 20 °C (Extended Data Fig. 2). 233

Moreover, density measurements confirmed that the micropores are hydrophobic enough at this 234

high Si:Al ratio to prevent water intrusion and form a microporous solution. This leads to an 235

extremely high measured O2 carrying capacity of 187 ± 18 mL/dL that, to the best of our 236

knowledge, far exceeds the capacity of any other natural or synthetic aqueous O2 carrier (Fig. 4c). 237

As an initial exploration of whether the high O2 carrying capacities of these microporous 238

liquids could be translated to more biomedically relevant environments than pure water, we 239

performed ex vivo experiments to test the delivery of O2 to deoxygenated donated human blood. 240

Importantly, density measurements confirm that the permanent microporosity of silicalite-1 and 241

(mPEG)ZIF-8 nanocrystals is maintained in a 5% dextrose solution (Extended Data Fig. 1), which 242

is isotonic to red blood cells (RBCs). The O2 carrying capacity of these solutions was extracted 243

from measurement of the change in oxyhemoglobin concentration upon addition of different 244

volumes of oxygenated solutions to deoxygenated RBCs. Notably, oxygenated solutions of 90-nm 245

silicalite-1 nanocrystals (10.8 vol %), 60-nm silicalite-1 nanocrystals (9.1 vol %), and 246

(mPEG)ZIF-8 (6.6 vol %) in 5% dextrose rapidly release O2 after injection into RBCs, with the 247

amount of O2 released increasing linearly in a dose-dependent manner. The extracted O2 carrying 248

capacities are in excellent agreement with the values predicted from adsorption measurements and 249

O2 release experiments in pure water (Fig. 4c, d). Additionally, more concentrated silicalite-1 250

colloidal solutions were capable of delivering 110 mL/dL of O2 to RBCs (Supplementary Table 251

30). 252

Overall, these results show how thermodynamic principles can be applied to bring the high 253

surface areas and gas capacities of microporous solids to aqueous fluids. This approach has 254

significant implications for biomedical and energy technologies, many of which are limited by the 255

transport of gas molecules through aqueous environments. For instance, the microporous water 256


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

concept could lead to novel electrolytes that complement or replace gas diffusion electrodes in 257

electrocatalytic reactions7, green solvents for acid gas separations36, treatments for decompression 258

sickness37, or injectable sources of O2 that could serve as artificial blood substitutes34, bridge 259

therapies for hypoxia induced by trauma38, or media for organ and tissue preservation39. Though 260

many factors beyond gas carrying capacity need to be considered in order to translate these systems 261

to viable technologies, there are myriad possibilities for designing hydrophobic zeolites and MOFs 262

with different crystal structures, nanocrystal sizes and shapes, and external surface functional 263

groups to create microporous water with high gas capacities and properties tailored to a specific 264

application. 265

METHODS General Procedures Nanopure H2O was obtained using a Milli-Q IQ 7000 water purification system. All compounds were synthesized and handled in air. All reagents were purchased from commercial vendors and used as received. Ultrahigh-purity grade (99.999% purity) He, O2, and CO2 were used for all gas sorption measurements. Hydrothermal syntheses were performed in Parr acid digestion vessels with PTFE liners. Sonication was performed using a 0.5-gal Branson CPX series sonicator with an operating frequency of 40 kHz. Calcination was performed using a STF1200 Across International tube furnace. Powder X-ray diffraction patterns were measured at ambient temperature using a D2 Phaser Bruker AXS diffractometer with CuK! radiation (! = 1.5418 Å). Material Syntheses Synthesis of 90-nm silicalite-1 nanocrystals. Silicalite-1 nanocrystals with an average diameter of 90 nm were synthesized following a procedure adapted from a previous report21. In a representative synthesis, aqueous tetrapropylammonium hydroxide (TPAOH; 31.51 mL, 40 wt %), H2O (40.52 mL), and tetraethylorthosilicate (TEOS; 38.36 mL) were combined in a 250-mL glass bottle. The initially biphasic mixture was stirred for 18 h, allowing the TEOS to become hydrolyzed in the alkaline environment and liberate ethanol (EtOH) into the solution. Following hydrolysis, the molar ratio of this solution was 9 TPAOH : 25 SiO2 : 480 H2O : 100 EtOH. The homogenous solution was loaded into a combination of 23-mL and 45-mL Parr acid digestion vessels, with each vessel filled to about 50% with the solution. These were sealed and heated to 90 °C for 48 h. After allowing the vessels to cool, the product was diluted roughly 10-fold with nanopure H2O and centrifuged at 7830 rpm (7197 rcf) for 80 min. The supernatant was then removed and washed 6 times with nanopure H2O. After the final wash, the sample was dried in a centrifuge tube at 60 °C overnight. The dried sample was collected and finely ground into a powder. About 3 g of powder was poured into alumina crucibles and loaded into a tube furnace. The powder was dried under flowing N2 by heating to 200 °C over 1 h and holding at this temperature for an additional 2 h. The powder was then calcined by heating to 550 °C over 1 h under flowing air and holding at this temperature for 10 h. The sample was then cooled to ambient temperature and collected. Synthesis of 60-nm silicalite-1 nanocrystals. In a representative synthesis, aqueous TPAOH (53.35 mL, 40 wt %) and TEOS (64.46 mL) were combined in a 250-mL glass bottle. The biphasic mixture was stirred for 68 h to allow for full hydrolysis of TEOS and aging of the solution. The molar ratio of the resulting solution was 9 TPAOH : 25 SiO2 : 380 H2O : 100 EtOH. Upon completion of aging, the solution was then uncapped and placed in an oil bath at 110 °C to evaporate the EtOH generated during hydrolysis of TEOS. Over the course of 2 h, the oil bath temperature was raised to 120 °C. After heating, the solution was re-weighed, and H2O was added to replace H2O that evaporated during heating and bring the molar ratio of the solution to 9 TPAOH : 25 SiO2 : 280 H2O. The resulting homogenous solution was loaded into 23-mL Parr acid digestion vessels, with each vessel filled to about 50% with the solution. These were sealed and heated to 80 °C for 48 h. After allowing the vessels to cool, the product was diluted roughly 10-fold with nanopure H2O and washed 6 times with nanopure H2O after centrifuging at 7830 rpm (7197 rcf) for 180 min and removing the supernatant. After the final wash, the sample was dried in a centrifuge tube at 60 °C overnight. The dried sample was collected, finely ground into a powder, and calcined following the same procedure as described for the 90-nm silicalite-1 nanoparticles.

Synthesis of high-silica ZSM-5 nanocrystals. ZSM-5 nanocrystals were synthesized following a procedure adapted from a previous report40. In a representative synthesis, aqueous TPAOH (5.552 mL, 20.3 wt %) and H2O (17.904 mL) were combined in a 250-mL glass bottle. While stirring, TEOS (27.104 mL) was added. Simultaneously, aluminum isopropoxide (495.8 mg), TPAOH (16.664 mL), H2O (5.968 mL), and NaOH (0.408 mL, 2.4 M) were added to a 50-mL round-bottom flask. The mixture was capped with a septum and heated while stirring at 85 °C until all the aluminum isopropoxide was dissolved. The Al solution was then cooled to room temperature and added dropwise while stirring to the Si solution. The resulting solution was then aged for 24 h at room temperature with stirring. After aging, the molar ratio of the resulting solution was 9 TPAOH : 0.1 Na2O : 25 SiO2 : 0.25 Al2O3 : 480 H2O : 100 EtOH. The solution was then partitioned into three 23-mL and two 45-mL Parr acid digestion vessels and heated to 90 °C for 60 h while rotating, with each vessel filled to about 50% with the solution. After allowing the vessels to cool, the product was divided evenly between 6 centrifuge tubes, diluted with nanopure H2O, and washed 12 times by centrifuging at 7830 rpm (7197 rcf) for 15 min. After the final wash, the sample was dried in centrifuge tubes at 60 °C overnight. The dried sample was collected, finely ground into a powder, and calcined following the same procedure as described for the 90-nm silicalite-1 nanocrystals. The final Si:Al ratio was 64:1 and the Al:Na ratio was 3.7:1 as determined by ICP-AES by Galbraith Laboratories. Synthesis of zeolite L (LTL) nanocrystals. In a representative synthesis adapted and modified from a previous report41, KOH (14.14 g, 0.252 mol) was added to H2O (45 mL) in a 100-mL glass jar with a PTFE stir bar. Then, Al(OH)3 (2.43 g, 0.031 mol) was added to the solution and dissolved by heating to 105 °C for 2.75 h, after which the solution became clear. The solution was cooled to ambient temperature, then HS-40 LUDOX (40%, 28.60 mL) was added while stirring. Within 30 min, the homogenous solution thickened and became opaque. The solution was left to age overnight with stirring, after which the solution became fluid again and had a moderately translucent blue hue. The solution was then loaded into 23-mL Parr acid digestion vessels, with each vessel filled to about 50% with the solution. The vessels were subsequently sealed and heated to 180 °C for 73 h, with each vessel filled to 40% with the solution. The product was diluted roughly 10-fold with nanopure H2O and washed 15 times with nanopure H2O after centrifuging at 7830 rpm (7197 rcf) for 180 min and removing the supernatant. After completion of the washes, the zeolite LTL nanoparticles were redispersed in enough H2O to bring the volumetric concentration to 9 vol %. The Si:Al ratio was 2.6:1 and the Al:K ratio was 1.1:1 as determined by ICP-AES by Galbraith Laboratories. Formation of aqueous solutions of silicalite-1 nanocrystals. To create uniform and stable colloidal dispersions, H2O (13.5 mL) was added to calcined 60- or 90-nm silicalite-1 nanocrystals (4.45 g) in a 20-mL glass vial sealed with a Teflon cap and sonicated for up to one week. Following sonication, the mostly translucent dispersion was transferred into a 50-mL centrifuge tube for further purification. The goal of this subsequent step was to remove any large aggregates that had irreversibly fused during calcination. To do so, the dispersion was subjected to a total of 25 centrifugation cycles; following each round of centrifugation, the supernatant was decanted and transferred to a fresh tube. The dispersion was first centrifuged at 1500 rpm (264 rcf) for 15 min to remove any large agglomerates, then centrifuged at 7830 rpm (7197 rcf) for 24 cycles ranging from 30 s to 1 min in duration. To concentrate the solution, the sample was split into two tubes and spun at 7197 rcf for 15 min to generate a nanoparticle-free layer of H2O on top. The final


<!-- Page 22 -->


22

concentration of the solution could be tuned by removing different amounts of H2O before redispersing the nanocrystals. Formation of aqueous solutions of ZSM-5 nanocrystals. To create uniform colloidal dispersions, H2O was added to calcined ZSM-5 nanocrystals (~3 g) in a 20-mL glass vial sealed with a Teflon cap and sonicated for a few days. Following sonication, the milky dispersion was transferred into a 50-mL centrifuge tube. The particles were washed 3 times with nanopure H2O at 7830 rpm (7197 rcf). Following washing, the particles were then size selected by centrifuging 2 times at 1500 rpm (264 rcf) for 15 minutes and discarding the precipitate. The dispersion was then repeatedly centrifuged for 2 min at 7830 rpm (7197 rcf), decanting the supernatant each time. A small amount of nanopure H2O was then added to the precipitate. Synthesis of ZIF-8 nanocrystals. ZIF-8 was synthesized in methanol (MeOH) following a previously reported procedure42. Briefly, Zn(NO3)2·6H2O (2.9 g, 0.0097 mol) and 2-methylimidazole (mIm; 6.5 g, 0.079 mol) were each dissolved in MeOH (100 mL). The two solutions were then mixed rapidly and stirred at 850 RPM for 1 h at room temperature. To remove excess reagents upon completion of the reaction, the solution was then subjected to 4 centrifuge cycles (25 min, 7197 rcf). After each cycle, the supernatant was decanted, and the remaining nanocrystals were redispersed in fresh MeOH. Synthesis of (mPEG)ZIF-8 nanocrystals. A suspension of ZIF-8 nanoparticles (80 mg) in MeOH (8 mL) was stirred at 500 RPM with triethylamine (0.5 mL) at room temperature for 20 min. While stirring, methoxypolyethylene epoxide (mPEG; PEG average Mn = 750 g/mol; 300 mg) was added. The solution was then heated to 45 °C and stirred for 3 days. To remove unreacted mPEG, the solution was centrifuged 4 times (20 min, 7197 rcf). After each cycle, the supernatant was discarded, and the resulting nanocrystals were redispersed in fresh methanol. The washed nanoparticles were dried under vacuum at 45 °C for 3 h and then re-suspended in water to form aqueous dispersions at different concentrations. Synthesis of ZIF-67 nanocrystals. ZIF-67 was synthesized in MeOH following a previously reported procedure (32).  Briefly, Co(NO3)•6H2O (1.44 g, 0.0094 mol) was dissolved in MeOH (200 mL). In a separate flask, mIm (3.24 g, 0.039 mol) was dissolved in MeOH (200 mL). The two solutions were then mixed and stirred at 800 RPM for 12 min, after which stirring was stopped and the solution was left at room temperature overnight. Nanocrystals were collected and purified by 4 centrifugation cycles (25 min, 7197 rcf). After each cycle, the supernatant was decanted, and the remaining nanocrystals were redispersed in fresh MeOH. BSA/ZIF-67 functionalization. Bovine serum albumin (BSA) with ≥ 98% purity was purchased from Sigma as a lyophilized powder and used as received. To use BSA to disperse ZIF-67 particles in H2O, the protein was first dissolved in H2O at a target concentration. Separately, dispersions of ZIF nanoparticles in MeOH were dried under vacuum. The dry ZIF powder was then added directly to the aqueous BSA solution, which was then sonicated and vortexed for 5 min at room temperature to facilitate adsorption and dispersion. Note that the protein crystal structure displayed in Figure 1D is of a BSA monomer. Nanoparticle Size Analysis Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Zeiss Ultra Plus) were used to quantify the particle size distribution of all synthesized nanocrystals. DLS measurements


<!-- Page 23 -->


23

were performed using a Malvern Zetasizer Ultra, while SEM images were acquired using a Zeiss Ultra Plus microscope. To prepare samples for DLS, a given colloidal solution was diluted with nanopure H2O to a final volumetric concentration of about 0.1–0.2%. Note that dilution is required in order to acquire accurate DLS data for samples at high concentrations. Particle dispersion and aggregation over time were monitored visually and by repeating the DLS measurement. The same conditions and instrument were used to run zeta potential measurements to characterize the surface hydrophilicity of ZSM-5 and silicalite-1. To prepare samples for SEM imaging, a given colloidal solution was diluted to a concentration near 0.1 mg/mL with EtOH and drop cast on Si wafers that had been previously cleaned by sonicating for 1 min in fresh acetone three times followed by sonicating for 1 min in fresh isopropanol three times. The SEM images were processed and analyzed using MIPAR. At least 100 nanocrystals were imaged to obtain average sizes for each sample. Concentration Measurements Nanocrystal concentrations were determined using one or more of the following techniques: inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and manual drying and weighing (Supplementary Table 3). ICP-AES measurements were performed for zeolite colloidal solutions by Galbraith Laboratories using method ME-70 after digesting samples with hydrofluoric acid. TGA measurements were performed on a TA Instruments TGA 550. Samples (20 μL) were pipetted into open Al pans with a stainless-steel bail under air and heated at a rate of 5 K min-1 to 600 °C under a 10 mL min-1 N2 flow with an empty Al pan and stainless-steel bail used as a reference. The TGA mass was calibrated using a series of 3 reference masses, while the TGA temperature was calibrated to the Curie temperature of Ni. For zeolite samples, the mass remaining at 600 °C was taken to correspond to the mass of nanocrystals in solution. For manual drying and weighing, a known volume of aqueous dispersion (typically 50–100 μL) was pipetted into a pre-weighed vial, dried at 130 °C, and weighed. To obtain the true mass of sample, the obtained mass of the sample was corrected for the amount of adsorbed H2O under ambient conditions as determined from the mass loss in TGA between 25 °C and 150 °C. All ZIF colloidal solution concentrations were determined by manual drying and weighing. Density Measurements Density measurements were performed using an Anton Paar DMA 4100 variable temperature density meter, which has an accuracy of ± 0.0001 g/mL. Prior to each measurement, the instrument calibration was verified at 20 °C and ambient pressure. Briefly, the density of ambient lab air and the density of nanopure water were recorded and compared to the expected values. A verification was deemed successful if the density of air was 0.0012 ± 0.0002 g/mL and the density of nanopure water was 0.9982 ± 0.0002 g/mL at 20 °C. After calibration verification, the sample cell was briefly dried using a built-in air pump to prepare for sample injection. For each measurement, a sample (1.1 mL) was injected into the sample cell, with the syringe left in the injection port to prevent movement of the sample or the entry of gas bubbles. The density of the sample was recorded at 15 °C, 25 °C, and 37 °C. The sample was then carefully removed using the syringe and diluted to obtain measurements at other concentrations. The sample cell was washed with at least 20 mL of nanopure water and dried with an air pump between each measurement. Viscosity Measurements An electromagnetically spinning viscometer (EMS-1000S, Kyoto Electronics Manufacturing) was used to measure the viscosity of the high-concentration dispersions of silicalite-1 and ZSM-5 nanocrystals. Specifically, 350 μL of aqueous solution was placed in a glass tube with a 4.7-mm


<!-- Page 24 -->


24

diameter Al ball. During the measurement, the Al ball was set to rotate with an input frequency of 1000 Hz. Rotation of the Al ball was traced with a red laser, and the viscosity was determined by the reduction in rotational speed. Each measurement was repeated 5–10 times at 25 °C, and the average is reported as the measured viscosity. Solid-State Gas Adsorption Measurements Solid powders were obtained by drying solutions of dispersed nanocrystals overnight in an oven at 130 °C. Powders were loaded into glass sample tubes and activated under vacuum overnight at 175 °C for post-calcined silicalite-1 and ZSM-5, 100 °C for pre-calcined silicalite-1, 120 °C for ZIF-8 and ZIF-67, and 75 °C for (mPEG)ZIF-8 using a Micromeritics SmartVacPrep equipped with a turbomolecular pump. Adsorption data was then recorded using a Micromeritics MicroActive 3Flex 3500.  Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface areas and pore volumes for each material were obtained from N2 adsorption isotherms at 77 K (Extended Data Fig. 3, Supplementary Figs. 3 – 7, Supplementary Table 4). Isotherm measurements near ambient temperature were performed using a recirculating dewar connected to an isothermal bath. Note that O2 and CO2 isotherms at 15, 25, and 37 °C were obtained on the same batch of material for which solution-phase adsorption measurements were performed (Extended Data Figs. 3 and 4, Supplementary Figs. 8 – 12). Gas Adsorption Isotherms for Aqueous Colloidal Solutions Adsorption measurements in solution were performed on a Micromeritics MicroActive 3Flex 3500 using a manual experimental procedure described below. We note that careful setup and analysis is required to obtain accurate gas sorption data using a volumetric instrument when the sample has a measurable vapor pressure, since the accuracy of the measurement relies solely on measurements of changes in total gas pressure. To ensure the accuracy of these measurements, control experiments for O2 and CO2 absorption in pure water were conducted at 25 °C (Supplementary Table 9). Experimental O2 and CO2 absorption amounts were compared to known solubility values in pure water to obtain a % of the expected value. The standard deviation across 3 independent runs of the % of expected value was used to obtain the error associated with the isotherm measurement. Oxygen Release Measurements in Deoxygenated Water Aqueous solutions were loaded into 2-mL or 4-mL glass vials, each equipped with a Teflon stir bar and capped with a red rubber septum with one inlet needles and one outlet needle inserted. Oxygenation was performed by flowing a continual stream of humidified O2 over the sample and was continued until the pO2 of the solution reached about 1 bar. The solution pO2 was measured using a contact-free fiber optic probe. Oxygen release into deoxygenated water was quantified with a Unisense MicroRespiration O2 microsensor. Briefly, nanopure water was deoxygenated by sparging with N2 for at least 30 min. A 2-point calibration was performed on the sensor prior to measurement of a specific aqueous solution. Specifically, the sensor was placed in fully nitrogenated water to obtain the mV reading corresponding to a concentration of 0 mg/L. Next, the sensor was placed in air-equilibrated nanopure water of a known temperature to calibrate the corresponding mV reading to the known mg/L (obtained from an O2 concentration table). After calibration, an aliquot of deoxygenated water was then sealed in an air-tight 1.2-mL measurement chamber possessing two gastight ports and a glass stir bar. Note that the measurement chamber was completely filled with water to ensure no headspace was present. The O2 probe was placed inside the measurement chamber through one


<!-- Page 25 -->


25

of the ports, and a baseline concentration (mg/L) was recorded. Then, a known volume of a nanocrystal solution was injected into the sealed measurement chamber, and the change in mg/L was measured to calculate the amount of O2 released into water. The temperature of the solution in the vial was also recorded either by directly inserting a thermocouple into the vial right after the measurement or by measuring the temperature of water in an adjacent vial. Oxygen Release Measurements in Packed Red Blood Cells To make the aqueous solutions isotonic with blood, enough dextrose was added to afford a final concentration of 5% dextrose (w/v). The samples were then oxygenated with 1 bar of O2 by sealing an aliquot of each solution in a 4-mL glass vial with a septa cap and piercing the cap with a needle. The vial was then placed into a 3-neck round bottom flask whose joints were connected to an O2 inlet with a H2O bubbler, a vacuum pump, and an oil bubbler outlet. The vial was continuously stirred, and three evacuation/refill cycles were performed on the sample. Specifically, the pressure was gradually decreased inside the flask over at least 15 min to 50 mmHg before continuing to evacuate at 50 mmHg for another 15 min. The total duration of evacuation was ~1 h. Following evacuation, the flask containing the samples was opened to flowing humidified O2 for 45 minutes. After three evacuation/refill cycles, the sample was left under flowing O2 overnight.
