A number of fetal anthropomorphic motion phantoms (FAMPs) gravid abdomen phantoms

(GAPs) for MRI have been developed in the past. Our lab has previously published a

quantitative analysis of these phantoms, evaluating them on their accuracy in meeting the four

requirements [18]. Through this review, it was found that there was an average accuracy of 26%

with 7% including sources of physiological motion [18]. Important to consider, some of these

and therefore have specific applications. Ideally, the phantom is comprehensive and is

composed of several tissue mimicking materials, accurately representing the complexity of the

Apart from the phantoms, there have been many products developed that are capable of

### 2.1.2 Robot Configurations

Most motion phantoms have 1-2 DOF because the anatomy they replicate is constrained by

surrounding tissues or muscles. Our fetal anthropomorphic motion phantom requires 6 DOF to

translate and/or rotate the fetus in any direction since it involves the entire body. In this

assembly, the motion created moves the entire fetus. The limbs are unable to function

independently as they would in a natural environment. This is due to the inability for the silicone

to have such a dynamic range of motion (ROM) and would require physical joints with actuators

to move each component. Since the boundaries of the different internal structures are the

regions of interest, the limbs are not substantially important. It is therefore sufficient to have the

limbs follow the body as it is moved, preventing the need for complex joints and actuation

methods integrated in the limbs. The most important parameter is the accuracy of the robot, with

other significant parameters being the workspace, speed, and the ability to distance actuators

from the phantom.

2.1.2.1 Serial Manipulators

The approach taken to design the robot is heavily influenced by its usage in the MRI. One

consideration is that positioning accuracy is vital which is somewhat challenging being unable to

use metals. Serial manipulators are known for their large workspaces they can reach in an open

loop chain. However, due to the sequential arrangement of the linkages and actuators, there is

an accumulation of error with each joint. This also makes it difficult to position the robot in the

MRI unless a horizontal orientation is used, maximizing the moment on the structure. Due to the

use of nonmetals in the construction, there would be a lack of stability as each link is being

supported by the previous one. This would further affect the accuracy and limit the accelerations

of the end effector. Lastly, it would be difficult to distance the actuators from the phantom itself,

making it difficult to avoid image artifacts.

2.1.2.2 Parallel Manipulators

By using a closed chain, the structure distributes the load across the several linkages for

enhanced stability. This also prevents mass and error from accumulating along each of the

linkages for improved accuracy and faster tool speeds/accelerations. Since all the linkages are

connected to the same end effector, this reduces the achievable workspace due to the

### 2.1.3 Transmission

After the delta configuration has been shown to be the best choice, an appropriate transmission

needs to be selected to convert the motion from the motors to the linear guides. The ideal

transmission is able to achieve high accuracies and speeds and be easy to set up in an MRI

environment.

2.1.3.1 Belt/Cables

Belts and cables are typically used in high-speed applications due to their lightweight and

smooth-running characteristics. Unlike gear trains, both belts and cables are easy to span

longer distances which can be helpful in separating the motors from the MRI. They don’t have to

be routed in a specific direction if more than one belt is being used, allowing for an extra degree

of control which is attractive. For example, if the robot is elevated, the belts or cables can still

route to the patient table so they are easy to mount. Challenges arise with set up and

maintenance since they must be tensioned properly for highest accuracy. Even with proper

tensioning, the elasticity of the belts or cables permits slack to affect the positioning accuracy.

Flat belts and cables are vulnerable to slip which can be avoided by using a timing belt where

the teeth would also help with changing directions.

2.1.3.2 Hydraulics/Pneumatics

Fluid can be forced through tubing to take advantage of Pascal’s Law to produce high force in

the output piston. Pneumatics uses pressurized air to accomplish this which is desirable

because it causes a minimal hazard in the case of a leak and requires lower maintenance

without the need for a reservoir. By using air, high speeds and accelerations can be achieved

due to the much lower mass and friction faced by the system. In contrast, hydraulics use liquids

as the fluid which changes many of the system’s characteristics. Hydraulics can produce much

stronger force outputs since they are far less compressible, although it is difficult to achieve

higher speeds and accelerations due to the increased mass and viscosity of the fluid. Both

options are as MRI friendly as it gets: they have an easy set up and the tubing can be run

through the waveguide with all electronics kept in the control room. Sadly, it is very difficult to

achieve a high positioning accuracy with them. Moreover, the pressures required to drive the

fluid through tubing at high speeds over long lengths is not practical according to the Hagen-

### 2.1.4 Actuator Selection

There are two classes of motors based on current type: AC and DC motors. AC motors are

generally used for continuous use applications due to their higher efficiency but suffer from

lower start up torque. Due to the use of sinusoidal currents, it would be expected to introduce

less noise in an MR environment since there are no sharp corners as there are in DC currents.

In contrast, DC motors have better position control and start/stop conditions. Since these are

essential to the project’s success, DC motors were selected.

Many types of DC motors exist: brushed, servo and stepper. Although they all use square

pulses to operate, several studies have shown to implement DC motors in an MR environment

[60], [61]. Brushed motors can be thought of as a bridge between AC and DC motors. They are

used for continuous high-speed RPM and are controlled by pulse width modulation. Servo

motors are known for high torque, speed and accuracy which is achieved through a closed loop

(servo) control system. They can further adjust their power according to a dynamic load,

however, DC servos are only capable of rotating <180°, due to the use of potentiometers. AC

servos work around this but are far more costly and complex to implement with performance

dropping largely around 300 hundred RPM. These servo control loops also introduce delays into

the system as it oscillates around the target value. Stepper motors move in discrete steps,

something which is unique compared to other motors. This ensures accuracy at a mechanical

level and helps with holding torque, or short movements. A trade off is made for lower efficiency

from high vibration and resonance. Although steppers tend to lose torque around 1000 RPM,

cost and control is far more manageable.

A special type of AC motor has been designed specifically for an MR environment. Piezoelectric

or ultrasonic motors are constructed from nonmagnetic materials, allowing them to be placed

anywhere in the MR scanner. However, they typically still introduce noise into images when they

are operating depending on how far from the region of interest they are. This is because they

use frequencies between 20 kHz and 10 MHz to create a controllable vibration, causing the

rotor to turn. Heat dissipation is a challenge with these motors because the mechanical

vibrations turn the rotor through friction between the surfaces. Similar to servo motors, a closed

2.1.4.1 Stepper Motor Principles

Since steppers have been chosen, a brief review of the underlying theory of operation will be

presented. In standard 1.8° stepper motors, a rotor has two wheels of 50 teeth: one at the north

pole and one at the south pole. The teeth are pulled to align with the stator, composed of two

rings of 48 teeth of the stator. The 48 teeth of the stator form groups of 6 with pairs being on the

opposite side of the stator as seen in Figure 2.2) Stepper motor anatomy. This causes one pair

of the rotor to be aligned with the stator, 2 pairs to be half aligned, and 1 pair to be unaligned.


<!-- Page 36 -->


23

*Figure 2.2) Stepper motor anatomy*

In full stepping, one coil consists of 4 electromagnets which are activated to make the teeth in

the stator with positive polarity, attract the teeth of the negatively polarized rotor (remember all

the teeth on one wheel of the rotor have the same polarity. Simultaneously, the negatively

charged teeth in the stator repel the teeth of the rotor, causing them to be unaligned. This

leaves the passive teeth of the other coil half aligned. Upon activating the other coil, the half-

aligned teeth are pulled to be fully aligned in the same manner. Micro stepping can be achieved

by effectively using the teeth on the other side of the rotor with different polarity and activating

the coils to align between positions. Due to the smaller steps, micro stepping can achieve higher

resolution and reduced noise which can be beneficial, especially at lower speeds. Although due

to the teeth being pulled between the electromagnets, torque is reduced as seen in the table

2.1.4.2 Quadrature Encoding

Motors are commonly paired with encoders in high precision applications to ensure the target

positions are reached. Optical rotary encoders are composed of a disc, light, photo detectors,

and a signal conditioner for analog to digital conversion. An LED shines through the disc with

alternating open and closed slots with the detector on the opposite side. Quadrature encoding is

a technique used by incremental encoders to determine the relative position and direction of the

rotor. The code wheels are carefully designed so that two channels are offset by 90° which

allows for 4 possible states depending on the edge transitions. By comparing the previous state

to the current state, the direction can be determined according to a truth table such as that

shown in Table 2.6) Quadrature encoding truth table.

### 2.1.5 Fixation method

In some way the fetus must be fixed to the end effector, and the placenta to the tank. The focus

of the phantom is to preserve the boundary of the fetus in the images. Hence a shaft will be


<!-- Page 41 -->


28

inserted into the fetus to reduce the surface area that is taken up by the supportive structure.

Importantly, it will be inserted in a region that is not near a region of interest and also can bear

the weight of the phantom sufficiently. Alternatively, a lattice like structure could be created to fix

to the fetus, but the increased surface area will displace amniotic fluid, and can deform the

boundary as it moves around which is undesirable. This shaft is fixed to the fetus by a sealant or

adhesive to prevent amniotic fluid from entering the gap between the fetus and shaft and will

consequently fix the shaft to the fetus.

To optimize the use of the space in the tank, the placenta could be fixed to either the side or

bottom of the tank. This can be accomplished in a similar manner to the fetus by using two small

pins which can be inserted into brackets on the tank. This ensures it can be removed but will still

be fixed in place during usage. Both phantoms will be placed in the appropriate location in the

tank by incorporating the bores of the shaft in the molds at the precise locations.

### 2.1.6 Material Selection

It is imperative to choose the best suited materials to construct the parts in order to maximize

the product’s effectiveness. This complex selection process considers a number of factors and

trade offs depending on the application of the design. For the MR compatible robot, there are

several properties that need to be contemplated:

- Elastic modulus: high stiffness is required to achieve high positioning accuracy

- Electrical conductivity: low conductivity will avoid eddy currents

- Chemical stability:  materials should be inert and non reactive to the amniotic fluid

- Friction: low friction coefficients are ideal for parts experiencing wear through motion

- Hardness: increases wear resistance and longevity

- Manufacturability: parts are ideally easy to make from standard processes

- MR compatibility: minimal interaction with magnetic fields as discussed in section

1.5.2.3.

- Tensile strength: high strength prevents plastic deformation under loading

- Water absorption: low water absorption preserves the part shape and integrity

As per 1.5.2.3, the MR environment prohibits the use of metals in the robot which is not ideal

because plastics have far weaker mechanical properties than metals. This does however allow

3D printing processes to be taken advantage of to produce custom made parts given the low

volume of production.

### 2.2 Mechanical Design

### 2.2.1 Iterations and Rationale

2.2.1.1 Version 1

The first iteration of the device was influenced by the triple scissor scaffold presented in Figure

2.10. It was chosen because it was believed the unique spherical joints connecting to the

platform and the carriages would allow for a larger range of motion compared to standard ball

and socket joints. After the CAD was developed, it was found that many of the parts would

require tight tolerances and would in general be very difficult to manufacture accurately. A

sample linear guide was 3D printed and the square rails were found to require tight tolerances

to slide smoothly, often getting stuck or being too loose even though the corners were

chamfered.

Piezoelectric motors were planned to be housed on the outside of the tank to reduce the length

of the transmission and allow the motors to be placed at the entrance of the bore with the

phantom at the isocenter. However, this introduced a number of complexities. Firstly, none of

the guides could exit through the top of the tank; even if a lid was used it would be unstable and

difficult to remove. This resulted in one guide coming out the bottom, requiring the entire tank to

be elevated and limiting the size of the robot. This also forced the robot to be configured

sideways, largely increasing the moment the phantom exerts on it and concentrating more force

on the vertically oriented guide. Further, by having the transmissions exit the tank at an angle to

couple with the motors on the exterior, manufacturing was made difficult. Several components

would be required to support the motors in strange angles and positions. A hole would also

have to be drilled in the glass tank to make a port for the driving shafts to penetrate which was

planned on being sealed with a rotary seal.

2.2.1.2 Version 2

The second iteration was focused on improving upon the linear guides and scissor mechanisms.

### 2.2.3 Workspace Analysis

The workspace of parallel robots is generally restricted by:

- Limitations of the actuated joints: the min and max values the guides can travel

- Limitations of the passive joints: the clevis and U joints

- Mechanical interferences between bodies

Typically, the forward kinematics equation is used to iteratively find the different nodes the end

effector can reach, forming a volume. In the case of parallel robots, the forwards kinematics

solution is excruciatingly difficult and so it was accomplished by moving the end effector to a

series of positions where the guides could no longer travel any further (Figure 2.16 & Figure

2.17). After performing the analysis in the SolidWorks assembly, some observations were

made.

- When homed, the workspace is a circle in the horizontal plane

- The carriages become closer or further from the origin when the height extends above or

below respectively, creating directional biases and skewing the workspace

- The guide limit is reached fastest when traveling directly along the carriage axis. This

becomes the limiting factor since the other guides can move more

- The workspace is defined by whichever is larger from the following

- Draw a tangent line from the inner circle perpendicular to the carriage axis. This

prevents the limiting guide from traveling any further

- Draw a line from the max value between the adjacent pair of guides and the min

value along one of the pair of guides

not supplemented with wire since they were connected to the ground plane and not a specific

trace. In terms of routing, traces were kept as short and straight as reasonably possible to

minimize resistance. Traces carrying larger currents were placed on the top layer to improve

heat dissipation.

Limit switches were configured with the common (C) pin connected to ground, and normally

open (NO) pin connected to a digital pin for a default high state. This way it is easy to debug if a

connection is made improperly or if it is loose. Later in the project, it was found that several of

the switches’ NO pin never closed, resulting in an always high state. The pins were then

reconfigured to grounded C pin and the NC pin was connected to the Arduino for a default low.

When the switch was closed, it only went to 0.2 V compared to an expected 3.3 V so pull up

resistors were added to resolve this issue.

2.3.2.1 Circuit protection

While most components are trivial, the power protection components required some planning.

The relay isolates the power to the drivers from the power applied to the board to prevent

damage to the drivers or Arduino in the case the motor power is reversed. This short circuits the

24 V to ground. The relay is a single pole single throw, normally open (SPST-NO) switch that is


<!-- Page 64 -->


51

triggered by the toggle switch supplying the power current to the coil side of the relay. The

current supplied to the power switch is drawn from a P-FET that only conducts if the 24V and

ground are appropriately configured. This was accomplished by making the P-FET conduct

between -1.3 to -2.3 V; if the polarity of the motor power is reversed, it will become positive,

hence it will not conduct past this point. A Zener diode with a current limiting resistor between

the gate and source to prevent the voltage from dropping below -10 V. Two capacitors store the

majority of charge that is available to the drivers, ensuring the motor power is not affected by

current spikes. These components were sourced to accommodate all 6 motors continuously

running at their rated current without exceeding a 20 °C rise in temperature.

The PCBs were designed in Altium (Altium Limited, San Diego, California, US) according to the

above criteria. The resulting schematics are shown below in Figure 2.24 and Figure 2.25 with

### 2.4.1 Position Planning UI

Another MATLAB application was developed to assist with the position planning of the robot.

While path planning generally consists of position, speed and acceleration relations between the

end effector and active joints, this app is only capable of having the end effector reach targets

and not provide an accurate model of the path taken to reach these targets. With six pose

parameters to define for each point in time, there is a lot of information that needs to be inputted

and processed to create a motion profile. This information was broken down into several

components as shown in Figure 2.27 and Figure 2.28. A motion profile is defined by a routine; a

full path to travel. The routine consists of one or more splices, each defining an end target and a

base function to get there for each of the pose parameters (Pxyz and Rxyz). While each routine

has a unique sampling frequency, each splice has a duration which defines the speed. A

sampling frequency is only required when a sine function is used in one or more of the pose

parameters in any of the splices. It discretizes the curve into nodes for the robot to move to and

prevents the need to interpolate a linear function.


<!-- Page 68 -->


55

*Figure 2.27) Signal Lab position planning UI.*

Linear functions only require a distance to travel. Sine functions are more complex since they

require more parameters to define them, including the amplitude (A), frequency (w), phase shift

(p) and vertical offset (b). Technically, sine functions can end anywhere according to the

definition (not necessarily where they started from) and a sequential function could begin at this

arbitrary location, however there is currently no error checking that would prevent a user from

starting the sequential function from a point not connected to the end of the previous sine

function. There is however, no way to start the sine function at an arbitrary location at this time,

that is, it always begins from the midline. The home function will pull the pose parameter from

wherever it is back to home and the delay function will keep the pose parameter at its current

location.

### 2.4.2 Robot Control

There are a few requirements that must be satisfied to meet the functionality and safety

requirements of this project. The ability to upload preplanned paths from Signal Lab will largely

accelerate the setup process to make the best use of time. A homing function will be required to

initialize the position of the robot, otherwise it would be difficult to establish the positions of the

linear guides at the time of the system start up. A closed loop system will also be required in

case the robot misses steps during the routine. This is particularly important with parallel robots

to avoid singularities, apart from achieving high accuracies. Also relevant to parallel robots,


<!-- Page 70 -->


57

coordinated movement is necessary to avoid singularities, ensure a target path is followed and

maintain the stability of the phantom.

2.4.2.1 Version 1: Arduino Control

To begin coding, a library was selected to help easily program the steppers. There are three

commonly used libraries for these purposes: AccelStepper, SpeedyStepper, and FlexyStepper.

Each of these libraries have been used in a few references for similar applications with

AccelStepper being the most common [67]–[74]. AccelStepper was originally selected due to its

built-in functions for controlling multiple motors for coordinated movements, however, it was

discovered that it is unable to use acceleration in these movements. A custom function was

developed to create coordinated movements in SpeedyStepper, but could handle accelerations

in these types of movements. It also supported arguments for different units like steps or

distances which was found helpful. According to its documentation, SpeedyStepper can reach

12 500 steps per second or 3750 RPM with an Arduino Uno which has a clock speed of 16

MHz. This means with 6 motors running at max speed will be at most 3750/6=625 RPM.

However, the Arduino Due has a clock speed of 84 MHz, providing 625*(84/16)=3281 RPM for

all 6 motors simultaneously. This is far superior compared to the max of 7000 and 4000 steps

per second on an Arduino Uno offered by FlexyStepper and AccelStepper respectively and will

therefore meet our requirement of 587 RPM as outlined in section 2.2.4. The PCBs were

designed to have motors mounted from number 1 to 6 from left to right. This is somewhat

conflicting with the numbering of the robot linkages which start at the back left link and progress

clockwise. As a result, one coil was reversed in each of the middle motors, so all motors are

programmed the same. The encoders are also reversed programmatically in the setup function

to count in the same direction as the others.

There are three methods to implement the exported path from Signal Lab. One option would be

to save the path on an SD card and add an SD card reader to the shield; alternatively, the path

could be parsed from a txt or csv file from another script outside of Arduino and sent using the

USB connection; lastly the coordinates could be copy and pasted into the Arduino Serial Monitor

or hard coded. For a first iteration, this last option was selected to keep things simple and move

quickly.

Arduino’s Serial Monitor is very primitive. It doesn’t support the ability to add on features and

can only exchange data serially between the Arduino and host device. The script created had


<!-- Page 71 -->


58

coordinates hard coded to test a simple path moving the robot up and down 3 times. The

motors, encoders and switches are first initialized and the script prompts the user to enter ‘h’

into the Serial Monitor to begin homing. The homing function makes all the motors step to bring

the guides towards the central hub until their respective limit switch is pressed to make the

respective guide stop by issuing an interrupt. This process continues until all limit switches have

been pressed. The carriages are then brought to a home position, usually about in the middle of

the guide. The user is then prompted to enter “m” to begin the motion profile. The profile is then

executed with a notification sent every time a node is completed. For each node, the duration of

the movement and the target position are known so the speed can be determined with

maximum acceleration values used. The motion function also takes the fastest moving motor

and scales all other motor speeds and accelerations so they finish at the same time. In both the

homing and motion functions, the user may enter “p” at any time to pause the device. The

Arduino simply continues reading the serial buffer until a resume request, “r”, is sent. When the

path is completed, a notification is sent, concluding the script. An example figure is shown in

Figure C1.

2.4.2.2 Version 2: Arduino and Processing UI

To avoid hard coding the coordinates, a secondary script can be used to process and send the

data from the host computer to the Arduino through the USB connection. Processing was

selected as it can develop a GUI to improve the user experience while enabling several other

modes of visualization and information for the user. Unlike the Arduino serial monitor, the UI can

be customized to include buttons, graphics like limit switch presses during homing, and can

clear any items that are no longer needed in the panel. As such, a processing script was

developed to allow the user to open an exported path by inputting a filename to open and parse

the coordinates of the path. After parsing, the number of coordinates is sent to the Arduino. The

number of digits is unknown, and therefore an x is used as a delimiting character to notify the

Arduino it is done sending the data. For example, if 16 nodes were parsed, the script would

send 16x to the Arduino. The Processing script also detects values larger or smaller than the

length of the guide and clip them to the appropriate max or min value and issue a notification to

the user. Information is then sent per coordinate, consisting of the location of each guide and a

timestamp for when the target should be reached. These values are separated by commas, with

the end of a coordinate being terminated similarly by an ‘x’. Upon sending the information for the

last coordinate, ‘d’ is sent to notify the Arduino all coordinates have been sent. The text file has

the structure for one coordinate with each coordinate on a new line.

A closed loop system was also introduced into this version. The encoders issue interrupts each

time a step is made to count the steps. The actual counted steps can be compared to the

desired steps that have been programmed, and the difference can be corrected for. This is

performed in a while loop until the actual and desired steps are equivalent to avoid scenarios

where the motor may not correct for all the steps in one repetition. It was found that a minimum

threshold of 10 steps was required to prevent the motors from endlessly oscillating back and

forth between the same or similar values in an attempt to correct its position. Important to note:

these interrupts and closed loop routines are blocking functions so prolonged discrepancies

may introduce delays. This can prevent potential system damage from the other actuators

continuing to move and putting the robot in unintended positions or orientations with a

malfunctioning link.

### 2.5 Experiments

### 2.5.1 Feasibility of Imaging a Single 1A Stepper

Although literature revealed DC motors have been tested as discussed in Section 2.1.4, it was

desirable to confirm these findings since they are not widely used. As a feasibility study, the

goal of the study is not to quantify the impact of the motors on SNR or field homogeneities, but

to gather a minimal amount of information to determine whether the idea is worth pursuing in the

design. This study will determine if a stepper motor can be used in an MR environment, how far

it must be positioned, and what effects pulling forces from the MRI have on the motor.

Identifying artifacts in images will help guide development as to what cautions need to be taken

to prevent EMI such as shielding, Faraday cages, etc.

A single 1A DB14S421S stepper motor (SANYO DENKI AMERICA INC., CA, USA) was bolted

to a 1-inch-thick wooden board with no connections. The patient table was brought out of the

room and the motor with the board was anchored to the farthest end of the table using thick

rope. The table was slowly brought towards the MRI until it was in position to be docked. The

table was then docked into the MRI until it was in a scanning position. Safety hazards could

arise by the motor pulling into the MRI. Thus, during this experiment, extra caution was taken by

observing the ropes and motor wires for pulling and any movement.

Once in place, the motor was connected to the penetration panel of the MRI room through a

DB9 connector with an integrated low pass filter, 20 MHz cut off. In the control room, a cable

extended from the penetration panel to an A4988 driver through a breadboard with alligator

clips. Electrical tape covered the exposed portions of the connections but was not shown in the

images. The table was brought out to replace the rope with sandbags and straps. The motor

was programmed to spin at a constant 60 RPM, reversing directions every 10 rotations. A 4522

130 95954 water-based phantom (Philips, Amsterdam, Netherlands) was placed at the

isocenter with a 32-channel cardiac torso coil placed around it for imaging observed in Figure

2.31.

T1E TSE, T2E FFE, and thermometry scans were performed on a 3T Philips Intera (full

sequence details in Appendix B, Table B1) Sequence parameters. These scans provide a good

sample of how both relaxometry and thermometry images are impacted. Each scan was

conducted for the motor conditions: off, full step and 1/16 step.


<!-- Page 75 -->


62

A middle slice was taken from each image stack to be used for the analysis. After subtracting

the motor off image (reference) and full step or 1/16 step images, any pixel with intensity

changes of 30% is considered an artifact according to the ASTM F2119 report. A binary map

was created by calculating the percent change per pixel and saturating any pixel exceeding a

threshold of 30%.

### 3.2 Positioning and Orientation Accuracy

It is imperative that the robot has a high positioning accuracy to minimize error introduced in

images. It is also essential to have a high reproducibility, allowing for reliable results to be

obtained for experimentation. For these reasons, the pose of the robot was assessed. This


<!-- Page 85 -->


72

could be done in one of three ways: (1) using a stereo camera, (2) using a high accuracy

computer vision system, or (3) using a sensor, such as those used with an NDI field generator.

A stereo camera (4k USB ELP camera, ELP-USB4K03-mfv) was selected to be used given its

high accuracy and of <1 mm and low cost [75]. MATLAB’s built in stereo camera calibrator app

was used for checkerboard camera calibration. Distances were triangulated between the tool tip

and fiducial markers of known locations, but it was found to be difficult to achieve even an

accuracy of <2 mm. It is believed to have high error from poor lighting conditions, lack of focal

depth, and negatively impacted by the glare from the tank. In response to these issues, a field

generator (Aurora tabletop, 610388) was used to evaluate the robot. A 6 DOF sensor was used

to determine the pose of the end effector by taping the sensor securely into a channel of a 3D

coordinate system used as a tool. The sensor was calibrated to account for the offset from the

tool tip using the pivoting technique described in the user manual. The room was set up as

shown in Figure 3.9.

Summary of equipment considerations during setup

- Do not coil the field generator cable

- SCU, SIU separated >1 m from field generator

- Tool cables separated >30 mm from field generator cable

- USB cable is separated from all other cables

- RF communication equipment >300 mm from any components

- No other field generators within 10 m

- Field generator having no metal objects within a 1 m from hemisphere (including table,

wall, etc)

- Position the field generator more than 10 cm above the floor to prevent any metallic

interference

- The tank was elevated to account for the offset in the sensing volume of the field

generator

The sensor was mounted to the shaft of the robot in a tight-fitting groove and was taped in place

so it was unable to move. Calibration was then performed by pivoting the shaft around a fixed

point according to the documentation. There were no adjustments made between trials. A path

was programmed to position the end effector to a random value in the following order: three x

Upon moving the robot and taking a measurement, the reading furthest from the programmed

outliers were removed from the orientation data at >2 SDs from the mean. The error appeared

to be directionally dependent as the discrepancies increased along the X, Y, Z and combination

of axes respectively. Reasons for variation in the X and Y axes are unknown, but the Z axis was

expected to be lowest in error to match that of the positioning error. It was noted that specifically

for the Z orientation, after the robot executed a move and held the sensor in a static orientation,

the recordings fluctuated. This jitter in measurements explains the larger orientation error in the

Z axis.

Since there is considerable positioning error, this makes it difficult to accurately determine the

rotational error. The axes that the end effector actually rotates about will deviate from that which

is programmed for, substantially increasing the error. Additionally, achieving a high positioning

accuracy indicates the guides and end effector can accurately be controlled, and therefore

orientation accuracy will match it correspondingly. Therefore, the orientation error was

determined using the differences since a rotation matrix would not accurately represent the

transformation. Although the positioning and orientation requirements were not met, it is a

strong start for the first iteration of the device. In following tests, it might be desirable to mount

two perpendicular 5 DOF sensors to a dedicated rig to reduce the rotational jitter around the z

axis. Also, if the tank is slightly misaligned, it may result in the robot moving along a slightly

deviating axis compared to the world frame. Upon achieving higher positioning accuracies and

more reliable rotational z axis readings, a rotation matrix representing the system error can be

determined as shown below.

### 3.3 Maximum Speed Test

The maximum achievable speed operating all 6 motors simultaneously with no load conditions

was tested and recorded in Table B8. No load conditions were used because the motors require

some time to accelerate and the short linear guides would not provide sufficient time to reach

top speeds and take data samples. Simultaneously running all motors at a maximum speed is


<!-- Page 88 -->


75

not expected to happen during path execution but provides a reasonable worst case scenario

for the maximum stepping rates that can be achieved.

A script was set up to accelerate the motors until a maximum speed was reached. Upon

reaching the peak speed, the time was recorded from the crystal oscillator of the Arduino. After

making 20 rotations, the time was recorded again, and the motors slowed to a stop. The speed

can be determined with the start and end time of the 20 rotations since the number of steps per

rotation are known. The encoder values were checked to ensure there were no discrepancies

between the programmed and actual positions.

The trials are recorded in Table B8) Experimental data from maximum speed test showing an

average maximum speed of 523 RPM which is insufficient for the maximum simulated 587

RPM. Additional tests will be required for optimizing code and running the drivers at high

frequencies to meet this requirement, although it is unlikely for all motors to be simultaneously

running at the maximum rated speed.

## 4 Discussion

### 4.1 Comparative Analysis

There are four MRI compatible 6 DOF parallel robots that have been developed but not for

phantom applications. A summary of each of these designs alongside the design characteristics

of the robot developed in this work are presented in Table 4.1 below.

*Table 4.1) Comparison of the developed robot to 3 other MRI compatible 6 DOF parallel robots*

Each of the three other robots have been targeted towards procedures requiring the

manipulation of a needle with roughly half the load which is predominantly experienced in a

single direction. Additionally, reaching high speeds is not a priority. These differences in design

criteria allow for alternative actuation methods such as DEAs and pneumatics to be used. Due

to the use of a needle, a small amount of volume is taken at the end effector, permitting the

robot itself to be larger and, therefore, reach larger workspaces, especially for the Pneumatic

SG. The accuracies among each of the different designs are within 1 mm from each other

(disregarding the slider crank mechanism which only evaluated the accuracy of the actuators).


<!-- Page 90 -->


77

Only the pneumatic SG design quantified its imaging impacts and was able to achieve low SNR

degradations.

### 4.2 Limitations

The objectives of this thesis were to (1) design and build a six degrees of freedom (DOF) robot,

(2) assess the MR compatibility of the robot, and (3) evaluate the robot’s pose accuracy. To

measure the pose accuracy, a spherical phantom with a copper sulfate solution was used.

However, it inaccurately represents the target shape and material of the fetal phantom. Upon

synthesizing a fetal phantom, the impact of the robot on the imaging quality should be re-

evaluated for more contextual results since the amount of signal generated from the phantom

may be different. Additionally, the SNR measurement is subjective given that it is system

dependent due to the differences in operating principles for each MRI OEM as well as due to

natural drift in the magnetic fields over time.

Finally, the motion accuracy of the robot can be substantially improved by deriving the Jacobian.

This task will also permit computing the speed and acceleration at each point for complete path

planning which is required for accurate motion profiles. However, this was beyond the scope of

the current thesis but will be done in future iterations of the product.

### 4.3 Future work

Product development follows an endless cycle to allow for continuous improvement, hence,

despite everything completed to date, there are always aspects to build upon. Some of the most

urgent ones are listed here.

### 4.3.1 Robot Modifications

Carriage Joints

Upon reaching near straight angles along the vertical axis, the clevis locks up at its base

causing a fracture in the stem or pin mount (provide picture). Instead of having the 3D printed

disc at the base of the clevis, it can be replaced with the stem of the clevis in a bearing. This

reduces the friction from the large surface area of the disc and should prevent or at least reduce

the seizing of the joint.


<!-- Page 91 -->


78

Limit Switch Mounts

Currently triangular shaped plates are being used to mount the limit switches to the central hub

of the linear guides. This requires the limit switches to be placed on top of the hub with

extensions added to the levers so they are contacted by the carriages. The number of parts can

be reduced while increasing stability and accuracy through incorporating the limit switches

directly into the central hub at the level of the carriages.

Bearing Covers

Particularly at the U joints, the bearings occasionally pull out because of the angled forces and

vibrations exerted on them. Covers can be placed on the open faces of the housing to prevent

bearings from pulling out.

Motor structure

After the upgrades performed at the MRI site at the Hospital for Sick Children, the table end was

changed, no longer fitting the motor stand properly. The structure supporting the motors needs

to be redesigned to fit on the new table. Ideally, this stand would also be adjustable to fit other

patient tables. Aluminum T slotted bars may be a great way to provide strength and flexibility.

3D Printed Material

For this first iteration of the robot, all resin parts were printed in the standard resin. This was a

great way to test the functionality of the mechanisms but other materials are better suited for

some parts. Namely, the lead screws should be printed in the durable resin as it is the most

lubricous to reduce friction and wear. The rigid resin can also be used for some parts requiring

strength and rigidity with a smooth surface finish such as the platform.

Vibration Dampening

The steppers generate significant vibrations operating in full step mode. It would be desirable to

reduce the vibrations before they are carried through the electronics and driving shafts.

Vibration dampening sheets may be beneficial to use between the motors and the panel, or

vibration dampening shaft couplers.


<!-- Page 92 -->


79

### 4.3.2 PCB Modifications

Pin/Trace Optimization

Several modifications can be made to the pin assignment of the shield as touched on in PCB

and Accessories. Pin 1 can be routed to 16 instead. On the relay, the trace can be connected to

the NO pin instead of the NC pin to prevent the need for the bridge. Overall, the number of pins

used can be reduced by removing the redundancy that was included for testing purposes,

namely, the negative voltage encoder pins and the 5V for the limit switches.

A trace could be added to the drivers for active gain control. This will allow for the drawn current

to be controlled to match the torque required. By regulating the current drawn, heat dissipation

can be improved.

Although it hasn’t been tested, the implementation of pull up resistors on the breakout board for

the encoders and limit switches may help with the response of the components.

Connectors

Since the redundant pins are being removed, an entire DB9 connector is not needed, and since

they are stacked on the board, an entire stack can be removed with an existing NC. The area of

the board can be reduced and the remaining connections condensed since the motor

connectors all have a NC pin.

Soldering the 18 AWG wires to the solder cups of the DB9 connectors to make the motor cables

was largely undesirable. It was difficult to work with the apparatus and the connections often

broke, even after adding the back shells. Purchasing DB9 cables of appropriate gauge or using

a different cable with adapters is highly recommended.

The limit switches should use a connector instead of a terminal block on the breakout board.

The many thin wires are very tedious to work with and the terminal blocks take up a lot of space.

It would also simplify the breakout board housing if the GX16 aviation connectors could be

installed directly onto the board; at the time, no board mounted components could be found. It

might even be easier to cut out mounting holes in the board and solder wires into holes adjacent

to the connector.


<!-- Page 93 -->


80

Solder Mask

The top overlay can be improved by making things more clearly labeled to help with debugging

and setting up. It was especially a bit more challenging on the breakout board since the

connectors were not in order to help with proximity and routing traces. The +/- on the power

terminal block needs to be reversed.

Motor Power Traces

As mentioned in section 6.2) PCB, the motor power traces were undersized intentionally as a

quick fix. To prevent the need for soldering external wires, there are a couple of different options

that may be more reliable and user friendly. Bus bars could be used to route the power as one

option. Alternatively, power planes could be used on a 4-layer PCB, although it may even be

possible to have local power planes on a 2-layer PCB if carefully designed. This means only the

regions with the circuit protection components and those extending to the drivers would use

power planes, but the rest of the PCB would not. Lastly, using a motor with a reduced current

rating is also an option. It would not be ideal to increase the copper thickness since only a small

portion of the board would actually require such large thicknesses, the signal traces typically

use very small currents.

Forced Airflow

Mounting a fan over the drivers will help cool them to run at the rated 2A for long periods of

time. It is possible that the drivers overheated during testing after ~15 min of continuous

operation. It would be desirable to have them operate up to an hour as MRI scan sessions for

research purposes are usually a minimum of an hour long.

### 4.3.3 Software Improvements

User Interface

The Arduino and Processing scripts have provided a good foundation to allow users to visualize

key information and are more user friendly than the Arduino scripts alone. Many additional

features could be implemented in the future to enhance the user experience. In the case of

many experiments, it could be beneficial to home the robot and upload new paths without

exiting the application to save time. It would also be beneficial to have some sort of visual

feedback of the robot’s position as it executes the path such as a wire frame of the robot or a

simple coordinate system showing the pose of the end effector. For motion simulations, ROS

may be able to address our needs. It was recommended that to interface with the MRI, a trigger


<!-- Page 94 -->


81

line could be implemented for gated imaging procedures, widely expanding the possible modes

of experimentation with the phantom.

Script Optimization

There are some features that were challenging to add and therefore, never fully implemented.

Using micro stepping for accelerating the transmissions and then transitioning to full steps

allows for much smoother movement at low speeds, higher stopping accuracy, and still permits

higher speeds to be achieved. Using the SpeedyStepper and FlexyStepper libraries, it was

found that changing the steps per millimeter during movements caused a strange interaction

between motor speed being scaled and requiring acceleration to reach the newly scaled speed.

Changing the speed before the step size or vice versa was found to have the same result.

Sinusoidal motion exported from Signal Lab was found to be very inconsistent and create a

jittery motion. Root causes for this are unknown, although it is suspected that it may involve the

few steps that are required to reach the close together discrete points with a required

acceleration to reach the target speed.

### 4.3.4 Respiratory and Cardiac Motion

To incorporate respiratory motion in the phantom, a tube can be inserted into the chest cavity of

the fetus to pump air resulting in expansion of the chest. This tube must be flexible and be

sufficient length to allow the gross body movement. It should also be as thin as possible to avoid

introducing an image artifact by displacing amniotic fluid. While the respiratory motion can be

driven by a ventilator, the same concepts can be implemented for cardiac motion but driven by a

pump.

## 5 Conclusions

Birth defects are a serious problem that can impair the life of newborns and families. Fetal

diagnostic imaging has been slow to develop new technologies for overcoming motion related

challenges. The development of anthropomorphic motion phantoms shows great promise for

accelerating data acquisition, reducing research costs, and results in image processing

algorithms with improved reliability and more robust sequences. Unfortunately, few phantoms

incorporate sources of motion currently. Through this project, a research tool was developed to

house the peripheral phantoms of the gravid abdomen with a motion device to implement

physiological motion sources in the fetal phantom. This also entailed the development of a

shield for the Arduino, a breakout board, and three software components to assist the user in

position planning and robot control. The robot’s positioning accuracy was assessed to be ±2.1

mm, which is a reasonable starting point based on our literature review and comparative

analysis with other existing mechanisms. Nonetheless, the robot dynamics can be improved

upon in future works by deriving and utilizing the Jacobian. This robotic mechanism which is

targeted as a research tool has been shown to only degrade image SNR by less than 2% at 3T

and a maximum B0 variation of 1 ppm, supporting its MR compatibility and minimal EMI.

Prospective efforts will push towards achieving higher accuracies, additional motion sources,

and enhanced user experiences to achieve the highest standard and most comprehensive MRI

phantoms of the gravid abdomen.
